title: Episode 189: Jimmy Carter: The Hostage Crisis, the Killer Rabbit, and the Nobel Peace Prize (1979–Present)
description:
In the spring of 1979, while fishing in a flat-bottomed boat in Plains, Georgia, President Jimmy Carter was startled by an aggressive swamp rabbit swimming furiously toward his canoe, shooing it away with a wooden paddle. When press secretary Rex Granum mentioned the encounter to a reporter, the media exploded into a feeding frenzy over the hilarious folklore of the 'Killer Rabbit.' Yet behind the laughter lay an agonizing season of geopolitical peril. On November 4, 1979, radical Iranian students stormed the U.S. Embassy in Tehran, seizing fifty-two Americans for four hundred and forty-four harrowing days. Carter refused to leave the White House, lighting no Christmas tree and bearing the tragic heartbreak of the Desert One rescue failure. Defeated by Ronald Reagan in 1980, Carter embarked on the most inspiring, celebrated post-presidency in world history: picking up hammers with Rosalynn for Habitat for Humanity, virtually eradicating Guinea worm disease worldwide, and earning the 2002 Nobel Peace Prize. Discover the immortal legacy of America's longest-lived president.

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we conclude our Jimmy Carter saga. While his final year in office was engulfed by international crisis and bizarre media sensationalism, Carter's post-presidency redefined what it means to serve humanity. Here is George with the story of the swamp rabbit, the Iranian desert tragedy, and the Nobel Peace Prize.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE INFAMOUS 'KILLER RABBIT' FOLKLORE
In April 1979, an innocent afternoon on a Georgia pond gave rise to one of the most absurd and hilarious media sensations in White House history. While enjoying a quiet solitary fishing trip in a flat-bottomed aluminum jon boat near Plains, President Carter spotted a large marsh rabbit swimming frantically through the murky water directly toward his boat. Hissing with bared teeth and flaring nostrils, the terrified creature attempted to climb aboard the gunwale. Recognizing that the animal was panicked and might bite, Carter used his wooden paddle to splash water at the rabbit until it turned and swam safely back to shore. Several months later, White House Press Secretary Rex Granum casually mentioned the odd incident over drinks with Associated Press reporter Brooks Jackson. The Washington Post ran a sensational front-page headline on August 30: 'President Attacked by Rabbit.' Editorial cartoonists had a field day, drawing Carter fleeing from giant, fanged, carnivorous bunny monsters. When the White House released an authentic photograph taken by a Navy photographer showing Carter splashing water at the swimming rabbit, the 'Killer Rabbit' was permanently etched into American political folklore—an amusing distraction in an era of gathering storm clouds. The hilarious rabbit folklore became an affectionate part of American political legend, showing how the intense media spotlight can magnify the most innocent personal encounters into worldwide news. The media's humorous fascination with the swamp rabbit showed how folklore and quirky anecdotes can humanize leaders during times of great stress.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE 'MALAISE' SPEECH: JULY 1979
In the summer of 1979, the United States was gripped by double-digit inflation, skyrocketing interest rates, and crippling gas lines sparked by the Iranian Revolution. Retreating to Camp David for ten solitary days, Carter met with dozens of civic leaders, labor officials, sociologists, and ordinary citizens to diagnose the national funk. On July 15, 1979, Carter addressed sixty-five million Americans on live television in what became known as the 'Malaise Speech'—though Carter never once uttered the word 'malaise.' In an astonishingly candid, philosophical sermon, Carter diagnosed what he termed a 'crisis of confidence' in the American soul: 'The symptoms of this crisis of the American spirit are all around us. For the first time in the history of our country, a majority of our people believe that the next five years will be worse than the past five years... Too many of us now tend to worship self-indulgence and consumption.' The speech initially received enthusiastic public acclaim, but when Carter abruptly asked for the resignations of his entire cabinet forty-eight hours later to reorganize his administration, the public panicked, viewing the reshuffle as a sign of chaos and paralysis. That unvarnished diagnosis of the national spirit urged Americans to look beyond material consumerism and rediscover the foundational communal virtues of citizenship and shared sacrifice. Carter's speech reflected his courage to speak uncomfortable truths to the American public, challenging the nation to live up to its highest moral ideals.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: FOUR HUNDRED AND FORTY-FOUR DAYS: THE IRAN HOSTAGES
On November 4, 1979, international catastrophe struck. In Tehran, hundreds of radical Islamist student militants stormed the United States Embassy, furious that Carter had permitted the deposed, cancer-stricken Shah of Iran into the United States for medical treatment. Fifty-two American diplomats and military guards were blindfolded, tied up, and paraded before television cameras, beginning a four-hundred-and-forty-four-day hostage ordeal that held the superpower hostage. Nightly television broadcasts, led by Ted Koppel's new ABC program 'Nightline,' counted the days with grim graphics: 'America Held Hostage: Day 100... Day 200.' Carter adopted the 'Rose Garden Strategy,' refusing to travel or campaign for re-election while American citizens remained captive. He left the National Christmas tree dark except for the top star, held daily prayer vigils in the Oval Office, and resisted fierce political demands from hawks to bomb Iranian oil fields, knowing that military strikes would result in the immediate execution of every American hostage. Carter's refusal to bomb Iranian targets protected the lives of the fifty-two hostages, prioritizing the survival of individual American citizens over domestic political expediency. His patient restraint during the four hundred and forty-four days kept the hostages alive, defying political pressure for rash military escalation.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE TRAGEDY OF DESERT ONE: APRIL 1980
By April 1980, after five agonizing months of diplomatic stalemate, Carter reluctantly approved 'Operation Eagle Claw'—a daring, highly complex military rescue mission. Elite Delta Force commandos led by Colonel Charlie Beckwith were to fly by eight Navy RH-53D Sea Stallion helicopters from the carrier USS Nimitz to a remote desert airstrip code-named 'Desert One' in central Iran, rendezvous with C-130 tankers, drive concealed in trucks into Tehran, and storm the embassy compound. But from the outset, the mission was cursed by horrific misfortune. A blinding desert dust storm known as a 'haboob' disabled three helicopters, reducing the operational fleet below the minimum six required. Beckwith recommended aborting the mission, and Carter concurred. But as the aircraft prepared to withdraw in the swirling darkness, a helicopter collided with an EC-130 tanker aircraft, igniting a colossal fireball of aviation fuel and ammunition. Eight brave American servicemen were killed in the desert sands. Carter went on live television the next morning with tears in his eyes, taking sole, unreserved personal responsibility for the tragic failure. The tragic disaster at Desert One broke Carter's heart, yet his immediate, unreserved acceptance of full personal responsibility exemplified the highest standard of presidential accountability. Carter's transparent honesty in addressing the tragic Desert One failure showed the profound moral accountability that defined his entire public life.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE MIRACLE RELEASE ON INAUGURATION DAY: 1981
Crushed by the hostage crisis, forty-four percent inflation, and a divided party, Carter was overwhelmingly defeated in the November 1980 presidential election by charismatic Republican nominee Ronald Reagan. Yet in his final seventy-two days in office, Carter worked with heroic, non-stop dedication to secure the release of the hostages before his term expired. Working through Algerian diplomats, Carter negotiated the Algiers Accords, unfreezing nearly eight billion dollars in Iranian assets in exchange for the hostages' safe return. Carter went without sleep for forty-eight continuous hours in the Oval Office, fine-tuning the complex international bank transfers down to the final minute. In a petty act of vengeance, the Iranian regime held the transport plane on the runway in Tehran until precisely twelve-thirty-three on January 20, 1981—twenty minutes after Ronald Reagan took the oath of office—before allowing the aircraft to take off into international airspace. The following morning, President Reagan graciously dispatched former President Carter as his personal envoy to Wiesbaden, Germany, where a weeping Jimmy Carter hugged each of the fifty-two freed Americans, finally bringing them home alive. His heroic, around-the-clock negotiations in his final days in office ensured that every single American hostage was delivered safely home to their families without the loss of a single hostage's life. The release of the hostages on Inauguration Day brought profound relief to the nation and closure to an agonizing chapter in American history.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: HABITAT FOR HUMANITY AND THE CARTER CENTER
Returning home to Plains at age fifty-six, bankrupt and facing one million dollars in debt on his peanut warehouse, Carter refused lucrative corporate board seats and paid speeches. Partnering with Rosalynn, he founded the non-profit Carter Center in Atlanta, dedicated to advancing human rights, resolving armed conflicts, and eradicating neglected tropical diseases across the developing world. In 1984, the Carters donned work boots, tool belts, and safety goggles to volunteer with Habitat for Humanity, a fledgling Christian charity building affordable homes for impoverished families. For thirty-five continuous years, through the annual 'Jimmy & Rosalynn Carter Work Project,' the former President spent a week every year pounding nails, hauling lumber, and hanging drywall beside thousands of volunteers, personally building over four thousand three hundred homes in fourteen countries from India to Haiti. Photographed with a black eye and fourteen stitches after a fall at age ninety-five, Carter refused to cancel his shift, building houses in Nashville the next morning with a bandaged face and a hammer in his hand. The Carters' tireless work with Habitat for Humanity transformed millions of lives, demonstrating that genuine service to humanity is performed with deeds, sweat, and humility rather than titles. The decades spent volunteering with Habitat for Humanity showed that true leadership is demonstrated through service to the poor and vulnerable.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE ERADICATION OF GUINEA WORM AND THE NOBEL LEGACY
Carter's greatest scientific and humanitarian triumph was his near-total eradication of Guinea worm disease—a horrific, agonizing parasite that had afflicted three and a half million impoverished people across twenty-one nations in Africa and Asia in 1986. Distributing millions of simple water filter straws and teaching villagers hygiene, Carter's campaign reduced global cases by an astonishing ninety-nine point nine percent—down to fewer than fifteen cases worldwide today, poised to become only the second human disease in history completely wiped from the face of the earth after smallpox. In 2002, Jimmy Carter was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for his decades of untiring effort to find peaceful solutions to international conflicts, advance democracy, and promote economic development. Surpassing John Adams and Herbert Hoover to become the longest-lived president in American history, Carter entered hospice care in Plains in 2023 at the age of ninety-eight, surrounded by the red Georgia soil where his journey had begun. Jimmy Carter proved that an individual's true moral greatness is not defined by the fleeting tenure of political office, but by a lifetime of selfless, unfailing love for the human family. The near-total eradication of Guinea worm disease and the Nobel Peace Prize cemented Jimmy Carter's legacy as an immortal humanitarian whose life was an enduring beacon of selfless love. His life of ninety-eight years proved that an individual's enduring legacy is measured by the sum of human suffering eased and lives redeemed.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Jimmy Carter's extraordinary century of life proved that character, humility, and service to others outshine all the trappings of power. To succeed him in 1980, the American nation turned to the Great Communicator: Ronald Reagan. Next week, we begin our exploration of Ronald Reagan: the boy from Dixon, Illinois, the Hollywood actor, the 1981 assassination attempt and his famous hospital humor, and the economic revolution that reshaped the 1980s. Until then, thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
